extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners, especially those working with nonprofits and health care organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for practicing public relations in nonprofit, faith-based, NGO, museum/library/arts, and health care settings, with emphasis on strategy, stakeholder communication, privacy/regulatory compliance, branding, and employee communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause marketing should accomplish mutual goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause marketing partnerships should 'accomplish mutual goals, such as funding for the nonprofit and an enhanced reputation for the business, which can lead to additional sales.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'On Deck for the Cure' — cruise-ship walks, small registration fee, recognition of survivors, breast-health promotion, and donating 75 percent of money raised to the nonprofit; resulted in substantial donations and positive media coverage. Evaluate cause marketing by whether it produces measurable funding for the nonprofit and reputational/marketing benefits for the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause marketing design: product tie-ins and clear donation terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cause marketing projects involve the design and sale of customized products; these should specify how much of each sale goes to the nonprofit (e.g., '$3 for each shirt going to ACS').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether product-based campaigns clearly communicate the charitable contribution per sale, align the product/message with the cause, and provide transparency to consumers about fund allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations roles in faith-based organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith-based organizations rely on professional communicators to build relationships and respond to crises, conveying strategic messages, enhancing organizational reputation, recruiting new members, increasing donations, and strengthening followers' faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate PR in faith-based settings by its ability to manage crises, maintain reputation, support membership/donation goals, and align communications with religious mission and stakeholder expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libraries' public relations must address service and technology needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Libraries face PR issues such as increasing demand for technology in an age of budget cuts, providing services to mobile phone users, expanding job-hunting services, helping teens, creating courses and reading programs, and crisis planning (difficult patrons, censorship, workplace violence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good library PR identifies audience service needs, communicates program availability, plans for crises, and leverages committees or public information departments to manage issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Museums and arts groups should use events and media to attract audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Museums have opportunities in traditional and online media, fund-raising, special events/exhibits, and attracting younger audiences (example: 'Culture and Cocktails' events accompanying new exhibits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess museum PR by its ability to design experiential events, target younger demographics, secure media coverage, and generate fundraising and attendance outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprofits need PR to secure volunteers, donations, and public funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprofit organizations rely on effective public relations to attract volunteers and funding from donors and public/private sources; without it many nonprofits might close their doors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure PR success by increases in volunteer engagement, donation levels, public funding, and the organization's ability to communicate mission and services to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: NGO functions: advocacy, funding, technical advice, and mission focus
rubrics_metrics.description: A nongovernmental organization (NGO) typically advocates for public policy, provides funding, technical advice, and advocacy for people in need, focuses on a specific mission or cause, and relies on passionate volunteers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate NGOs' communications by how well they advance policy advocacy, mobilize resources, sustain volunteer engagement, and communicate mission-driven activities and impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: NGOs should shape attitudes, policies, and institutional accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: NGOs seek to impact attitudes, policies, and practices of decision makers and to make political and economic institutions more accountable; some NGOs integrate advocacy into humanitarian work to address structural causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether NGO messaging reframes issues toward rights/structural causes, influences policy debates, and holds institutions accountable with evidence-based advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect patient privacy and comply with health regulations (HIPAA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Health care public relations must protect patient privacy: HIPAA 'protects the privacy and security of patients’ health care information' and imposes strict limits on what information can be publicly shared; other regulations govern disclosure of patient-safety information and restrict false or misleading promotional practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR practitioners must partner with legal departments to ensure familiarity and compliance with HIPAA and related regulations; noncompliance risks significant fines or penalties. Communications should be vetted for privacy/security and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partner with legal on regulatory and fraud/abuse constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must partner with their legal departments to ensure they are familiar and compliant with regulations governing health care fraud and abuse, privacy, and promotional practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed legal review into messaging processes, especially when releasing patient-related information, promotional material, or patient-safety disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain health care complexity: costs, choice limits, and who pays
rubrics_metrics.description: Helping consumers understand controversial health care issues is challenging because payers often (insurers/employers/government) rather than providers control pricing, consumers often lack awareness of actual costs, and individuals commonly have limited choice of insurers, providers, or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective PR should clarify how costs are determined, who bears them, constraints on consumer choice, and the implications for care and premiums to reduce confusion and misperception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and tailor communication to diverse health-care publics
rubrics_metrics.description: The publics for health care PR extend beyond patients and include employers, referring doctors, regulators, policy makers, advocacy organizations, labor unions, and others; meeting their unique communication needs requires specialized PR skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment stakeholders, tailor messages and channels for each group, and prioritize communications that address specific interests (e.g., employers' cost concerns, clinicians' clinical evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridge clinical and consumer definitions of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Health care professionals often equate quality with clinical outcomes, whereas consumers equate quality with service and convenience; PR must bridge these differences while meeting demands of both groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop messaging that communicates clinical outcomes in consumer-relevant terms and highlights service/convenience improvements alongside clinical quality metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align communications with organizational operations and brand promise
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization's communications and its actions must be aligned; brand positioning and promotion are designed to predispose purchasers and receivers of care to select the organization, and effective branding should produce a lasting experiential feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess communications by their fidelity to operational reality (service delivery), consistency across channels, and ability to deliver the brand promise through both messaging and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trusted clinicians as advocates and spokespeople
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicians and other health care professionals are highly trusted and can serve as effective advocates/spokespersons; many public relations professionals cultivate relationships with physician partners for important messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate spokesperson strategy by clinician credibility with intended audiences (e.g., Gallup data: physicians 73% trusted), training/support for clinicians as spokespeople, and alignment of clinician messages with organizational goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand business, financing, politics, technology, and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: PR professionals must understand the complex business and financing of health care—how politics, regulations, economic conditions, technological innovations, and financial incentives affect quality, costs, and stakeholder behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective messaging is informed by knowledge of reimbursement models, regulatory environments, EMR/technology impacts, and incentive structures; PR should coordinate with strategy and operations teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee communication strategy to drive engagement and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-planned and well-executed employee communication strategy promotes employee engagement and positively influences and aligns the messages employees convey externally, which affects retention, absenteeism, patient safety, patient care outcomes, patient satisfaction, and brand reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure internal PR by employee engagement metrics, retention/absenteeism rates, patient-safety indicators, and the extent to which employees act as aligned brand ambassadors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish media and social media policies for employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Most organizations have policies that discourage employees from directly interacting with the media and encourage or require them to contact the public relations department; organizations are also developing social media policies because communicating via social media is no different than talking to traditional media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement clear media/social media policies, provide training, and ensure employees understand responsibilities and reporting channels; publish policies where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accessible internal communication channels for frontline workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Frontline health care workers often lack desk/desk-top intranet access and rely on written newsletters, bulletin-board announcements, break-room flyers, in-person meetings, computer kiosks in public areas, external websites (blogs/podcasts), and smart phones to receive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design internal communications with frontline accessibility in mind: multiple low-technology channels, supervisor-mediated communication, kiosks, mobile-friendly content, and off-firewall resources for home access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated communication: use research, planning, and multiple tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Health care PR professionals use research and analysis, strategic communication planning, and a wide variety of tactics (news releases, media statements, press conferences, online engagement, partnerships, sponsorships, newsletters, speakers) to support brand positioning and protect reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate integrated campaigns by coherence across tactics, evidence-based strategy, measurement of reach and impact, and the ability to mitigate negative perceptions while reinforcing brand strengths.
